title: The King James Bible Committees
text:
In January 1604 King James I met church leaders at Hampton Court Palace. The Puritan scholar John Rainolds suggested a new English translation of the Bible, and the king, who disliked the popular Geneva Bible and its notes, agreed.

About fifty scholars were divided into six companies, two each at Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge, and each company was given a section of the Bible. Archbishop Richard Bancroft issued a set of rules. The translators were to follow the existing Bishops' Bible where it was accurate, keep familiar church words, and add no marginal notes except to explain Hebrew or Greek.

The rules also set out a system of review. Each member of a company translated the same chapters on his own. The company then met to compare versions and agree on one. Each finished book was sent to the other companies for comment, and disagreements were settled at a general meeting. In 1610 a small committee met in London to review the whole text.

The translators borrowed heavily from earlier versions, above all William Tyndale's. Their preface, written by Miles Smith, said they had not set out to make a new translation, but to make a good one better. The King James Version appeared in 1611. Its language, much of it inherited from Tyndale and polished by the committees, shaped English prose for centuries.
lesson: A committee can produce excellent work when it has clear rules, independent drafts and real review. Structure the process so that every draft gets tested by fresh eyes.
people: King James I, John Rainolds, Richard Bancroft, Lancelot Andrewes, Miles Smith
location: Westminster, Oxford and Cambridge, England, United Kingdom
source: 'The Translators to the Reader', preface to the King James Bible (1611); Adam Nicolson, Power and Glory (2003)
